paragraphs.text:
1. Cynthia first ensnared me, wretched, with her eyes,
untouched until then by any desire.
Then Love cast down the look of my steady pride
and pressed my head beneath his planted feet,
till he taught me, the scoundrel, to loathe chaste girls
and to live with no plan to guide me at all.
Ah, this madness has not let go for a whole year now,
and still I am forced to find the gods against me.
Milanion, by shirking no labour, Tullus,
broke down the cruelty of hard Atalanta.
For now he wandered, witless, in Parthenian caves,
and now he went out to face the shaggy beasts;
struck too by the blow of Hylaeus' club,
wounded, he groaned upon Arcadian crags.
Thus he was able to master the swift-footed girl:
so much in love do faith and good deeds avail.
In me sluggish Love can think of no devices,
nor remember, as before, to walk the well-known roads.
But you who have the trick of drawing down the moon,
whose task is to work rites on magic fires,
come now, turn round the heart of my mistress,
and make her face grow paler than my own!
Then I would believe you can lead spirits and stars
wherever you will with Cytaean spells.
Or you, my friends, who call me back too late from my fall,
seek remedies for a heart that is not sound.
Bravely I will endure both the knife and the cruel fires,
if only I have freedom to say what anger wills.
Carry me through farthest nations, carry me over the waves,
where no woman may know the road I take.
You stay behind, to whom the god has nodded with kindly ear,
and may you always be matched in safe, untroubled love.
For my own Venus drives me through bitter nights,
and Love, never empty, fails me at no hour.
Avoid this evil, I warn you: let each keep to his own
beloved, and never shift the bed of accustomed love.
But if anyone turns dull ears to my warnings,
alas, with what grief he will recall my words!

2. What good is it, my life, to go out with hair adorned
and stir the thin folds of a Coan gown,
or to drench your locks with myrrh of Orontes,
and sell yourself off with foreign trinkets,
to ruin nature's grace with bought refinement,
and not let your limbs shine in their own good things?
Believe me, there is no medicine for your beauty:
naked Love does not love a beauty contrived.
Look at the colours the unploughed earth sends up,
how ivy comes the better of its own accord,
how the arbutus rises lovelier in lonely caves,
and the untaught stream knows how to run its course.
The shores gleam, painted with native pebbles,
and birds sing the sweeter with no art at all.
Not so did Phoebe, daughter of Leucippus, kindle Castor,
nor her sister Hilaira, by adornment, Pollux;
nor she, once the cause of strife between Idas and ardent Phoebus,
the daughter of Evenus on her father's shores;
nor did Hippodamia draw her Phrygian husband
by false fairness, carried off on foreign wheels:
but a face was theirs that owed nothing to gems,
such as the colour in the paintings of Apelles.
They had no eagerness to hunt lovers with rouge:
for them ample beauty was their chastity.
I do not now fear that you are cheaper to me than these:
if a girl pleases one man, she is adorned enough;
especially since Phoebus grants you his songs
and Calliope gladly her Aonian lyre,
and there is no lack of singular grace in your charming words,
all that Venus and all that Minerva approve.
By these you will always be most dear to my life,

3. As lay the Cnossian maid, languid, on the deserted shore
when the keel of Theseus drew away;
as the daughter of Cepheus, Andromeda, sank into first sleep,
now free at last from the hard rocks;
and no less as the Thracian woman, worn with constant dances,
collapses on the grassy bank of Apidanus:
so seemed Cynthia to me, breathing soft repose,
her head propped on hands clasped together,
when I dragged my drunken steps, heavy with much wine,
and the boys were shaking the torch in the late night.
Not yet entirely robbed of my senses,
I tried to approach her, pressing softly on the couch;
and though, seized by a double ardour, they bade me on,
Love on this side, Bacchus on that, both harsh gods,
to slip an arm beneath and try her as she lay,
and with hand brought near to take slow kisses,
still I did not dare to disturb my mistress' rest,
fearing the reproaches of cruelty I had known;
but I clung there, fixed with intent eyes,
as Argus on the strange horns of Io.
And now I loosed the garlands from my brow
and laid them, Cynthia, on your temples;
now I delighted to shape your fallen hair;
now I gave stolen apples into your cupped hands:
all gifts I lavished on ungrateful sleep,
gifts often rolling from your sloping breast;
and whenever you drew a sigh with rare movement,
I stood stunned, credulous of an idle omen,
lest some vision should bring you unwonted fears,
lest someone force you, unwilling, to be his:
till the moon, hurrying past the parted windows,
the busy moon with its lingering light,
opened your closed eyes with gentle rays.
Thus she spoke, leaning on her elbow on the soft couch:
'So another's wrong has at last brought you back to my bed,
shut out from her closed doors?
For where have you spent the long hours of my night,
worn out, alas, now that the stars are gone?
O that you, scoundrel, might pass such nights
as you always make me, poor wretch, endure!
For now I beguiled sleep with the purple thread,
and again, weary, with the song of Orpheus' lyre;
at times I softly mourned to myself, abandoned,
the long delays so often spent in another's love:
till Sleep pressed me, exhausted, with his pleasant wings.
That was the last care of my tears.'

4. Why, Bassus, by praising so many girls,
do you force me, changed, to leave my mistress?
Why do you not let me lead whatever life remains
with this servitude I have grown used to?
Though you should recall in praise the beauty of Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, and you
the Spartan Hermione,
and all that the age of beauty's prime has borne;
Cynthia would not let those bear the name of fair:
still less, if she were set beside lesser figures,
would she go off, by a harsh judge, the worse and base.
But this beauty is the least part of my madness;
there are greater things, Bassus, for which it is sweet to perish:
a natural complexion, grace in her moving limbs, and joys
it is sweet to learn beneath the silent gown.
The more you strive to break apart our love,
the more we both deceive you with a faith well kept.
You will not get off scot-free: this wild girl will know it
and will be your enemy with no silent words;
nor after this will Cynthia entrust me to you, nor will she
seek you out; she will remember so great a crime,
and, enraged, will defame you to all the other girls:
alas, at no threshold will you be welcome.
She will not scorn any altars in her weeping,
or any stone that is sacred, of whatever kind, wherever it stands.
By no loss is Cynthia more grievously tried
than when her glory ceases, with her love snatched away,
mine above all. May she stay so always, I pray,
and may I find nothing in her to complain of!

5. Envious one, restrain at last your troublesome words
and let us go, paired in the course we are in!
What do you want, madman? to feel my frenzies?
Unhappy man, you hasten to know the worst of evils,
and, wretched, to set your feet through unknown fires,
and to drink the poisons of all Thessaly.
She is not to be compared with fickle girls:
she will not know how to be angry with you gently.
But if by chance she is not opposed to your prayers,
what thousands of cares she will give you!
She will leave you now no sleep, now not your eyes:
fierce in spirit, she alone binds men fast.
Ah, how often, scorned, you will run to my threshold,
when your brave words fall amid sobbing,
and a trembling shudder rises from your sad weeping,
and fear draws an ugly mark upon your face,
and whatever words you wish flee you as you complain,
and you cannot, poor wretch, know who or where you are!
Then you will be forced to learn the heavy servitude
of my girl, and what it is to come home shut out;
no longer will you wonder so often at my pallor,
or why I am nothing in my whole body.
Nor will noble birth be able to help you in love:
Love does not know how to yield to ancestral portraits.
But if you give the slightest trace of a fault,
how quickly you will become a rumour from so great a name!
Then I shall not be able to bring you comfort when you ask,
since I have no medicine for my own ill;
but together, wretched, we shall be forced by shared love
to weep, each on the other's bosom in turn.
So cease, Gallus, to ask what my Cynthia can do:
not unpunished does she come when she is courted.

6. I do not now fear, Tullus, to learn the Adriatic sea with you,
nor to set sails on the Aegean brine,
with whom I could climb the Riphaean mountains
and go further, to the dwellings of Memnon;
but the words of my mistress, embracing me, hold me back,
and her grave pleas, with face often changed in colour.
All night long she chatters to me of her flames,
and complains, forsaken, that there are no gods;
she now denies herself to me as mine, now she threatens
what a sad mistress is wont against an ungrateful man.
Against these complaints I cannot hold out an hour:
ah, let him perish, whoever can love half-heartedly!
Is it worth so much to me to know learned Athens
and to behold the ancient riches of Asia,
that Cynthia should hurl abuse at the launched ship
and mark her face with frenzied hands,
and say she owes her kisses to the opposing wind,
and that nothing is harsher than a faithless man?
Do you strive to outdo your uncle's well-earned axes,
and restore old rights to the allies who forgot them.
For your youth has never had leisure for love,
but your care was always for your armed fatherland;
and may that boy never bring you the labours I bear,
and all that is known to my tears!
Let me, whom fortune has always wished to lie low,
yield up my last breath to this worthlessness.
Many have gladly perished in long love,
and in their number may the earth cover me too.
I was not born suited to praise, not to arms:
this is the warfare the fates would have me undergo.
But you, whether soft Ionia stretches before you, or where
Lydia wets the ploughed fields with the stream of Pactolus,
whether you traverse lands on foot or the sea by oar,
you will go, and be part of a welcomed government:
then if some hour comes to you not forgetful of me,
you will be sure that I live under a hard star.

7. While the Cadmean Thebes are sung by you, Ponticus,
and the grim arms of brothers' warfare,
and, so may I be happy, you vie with Homer himself
(if only the fates are kind to your songs),
I, as I am used, pursue my loves,
and seek something against my hard mistress;
not so much to my talent as to my grief am I forced
to be a slave, and to lament the hard times of my youth.
This is the manner my life is worn away in, this is my fame,
from this I wish the name of my song to spread.
Let them praise me for having pleased a learned girl,
Ponticus, and for having often borne unjust threats;
let the neglected lover read me diligently hereafter,
and may it profit him to know my woes.
If this boy too has struck you with his sure bow—
would that our gods had not let me be wronged!—
far from your camp, far, wretched, from your seven columns
you will weep, lying deaf in eternal neglect;
and in vain you will long to compose a tender verse,
nor will Love, too late, supply you songs.
Then you will often marvel at me, no humble poet,
then I shall be preferred above Roman talents.
Beware lest you scorn my songs in your pride:
often Love comes late at great interest.

8a. Are you then mad, and does my love not hold you back?
Or am I cheaper to you than icy Illyria?
And does that man, whoever he is, now seem so much to you
that you would go without me wherever the wind blows?
Can you, brave, hear the murmurs of the raging sea,
and can you lie on the hard ship?
Can you press the frost laid down with tender feet,
can you, Cynthia, endure the unaccustomed snows?
O that the time of winter's cold were doubled,
and the sailor idle while the Pleiades are slow,
and that the rope were not loosed from the Tyrrhenian sand,
nor a hostile breeze make light of my prayers,
and let me, rooted to the empty shore,
often call you cruel with a threatening hand!
But however, perjured one, you deal with me,
may Galatea not be hostile to your voyage;
and may I not see such winds subside,
when the wave carries off your departing ships,
so that, the Ceraunia conquered with lucky oar,
calm Oricos receives you on peaceful seas.
For no women will be able to seduce me from
lamenting at your threshold, my life, about you;
nor will I cease to ask the hurrying sailors,
'Tell me, in what harbour is my girl shut up?',
and I shall say, 'Though she settle on Artacian shores,
and though on Hylaean, she will be mine.'

8b. She will stay here! she has sworn to stay! let my rivals burst with envy!
I have won: she could not resist my constant prayers.
Let greedy envy lay aside its false joys:
my Cynthia has ceased to go new ways.
I am dear to her, and through me Rome is said
to be most dear, and without me she denies kingdoms can be sweet.
She chose to rest with me on a narrow bed
and to be mine in any way at all,
rather than the ancient kingdom of dowered Hippodamia,
and the wealth Elis had gained, well-suited to horses.
Though he gave great gifts, though he would give greater,
still she did not flee, greedy, from my arms.
I could not bend her with gold, nor with Indian pearls,
but I could, by the homage of a flattering song.
So there are Muses, and Apollo is not slow to a lover,
on whom I rely as I love: rare Cynthia is mine!
Now I may touch the highest stars with my feet:
whether day or night shall come, she is mine!
Nor will a rival steal my certain love away:
that glory will know my old age.

9. I told you, mocker, that love would come,
and that your free words would not last forever:
behold, you lie low, and come a suppliant to a girl's law,
and now any girl, bought just now, gives you orders.
The Chaonian doves cannot outdo me in love
at telling which young men each girl tames.
Grief and tears have rightly made me skilled:
and would that, my love laid aside, I might be called untaught!
What good now to you, wretched, is the singing of solemn song,
or weeping over the walls of Amphion's lyre?
In love a verse of Mimnermus avails more than Homer:
gentle Love seeks soft songs.
Go, I beg, and lay those grim little books aside,
and sing what any girl would wish to know!
What if you had no easy supply! As it is, you,
madman, seek water in the middle of a river.
You are not yet even pale, nor touched by the true fire:
this is the first spark of the evil to come.
Then you will long to approach Armenian tigers
and to know the chains of the infernal wheel,
rather than feel the boy's bow so often in your marrow
and be unable to deny anything to your angry girl.
Love has never lent his wings to anyone so freely
that he did not press him down with alternating hand.
Nor let it deceive you that she is willing enough:
the more keenly she comes upon you, Ponticus, if she is yours,
since it is not allowed to lead your idle eyes elsewhere,
nor will Love let you keep watch at another's door.
He is not revealed before his hand has touched the bone:
whoever you are, flee constant flatteries!
To them even flints and oaks might yield,
still more you, that light breath of yours.
So, if you have any shame, confess your errors as soon as you can:
to say for whom you are dying often eases love.

10. O pleasant quiet, when as a witness to that first love
I was present, sharing in your tears!
O sweet delight to remember that night,
O how often it must be invoked in my prayers,
when we saw you, Gallus, embracing your girl
dying, and drawing out long words in slow delay!
Though sleep weighed down my drooping eyes
and the Moon blushed in mid-heaven among her horses,
still I could not withdraw from your play:
so great was the ardour in your exchanged words.
But since you were not afraid to trust me,
receive the gifts of the gladness entrusted to me:
not only have I learned to keep silent your griefs,
there is something greater in me, friend, than faith.
I can join sundered lovers again,
and I can open a mistress' reluctant doors;
and I can heal another's fresh cares,
nor is there light medicine in my words.
Cynthia taught me what each must always seek
and what must be shunned: Love has done no little thing.
Beware of wishing to fight with a sullen girl,
or speaking proudly, or staying silent too long;
nor, if she asks something, refuse with ungracious brow,
nor let your kind words fall to no purpose.
She comes provoked when she is scorned,
nor does she remember, wronged, to lay aside just threats:
but the more humble you are and subject to love,
the more often you may enjoy a good outcome.
He will be able to remain happy with one girl
who is never free with an empty heart.

11. Does any thought of us come, Cynthia, lingering amid Baiae,
where the path lies along the Herculean shores,
and now marvelling at the waters laid beneath Thesprotus' realm,
close to noble Misenum,
to bring back nights mindful of our love?
Does any place remain in the farthest reach of your love?
Or has some enemy, with feigned flames,
torn you, Cynthia, from my songs,
as a girl is wont to slip when her guardian is removed,
faithless, and to forget the gods we share?
Would that a tiny skiff, trusting to slender oars,
might rather keep you on the Lucrine water,
or that the wave, easy to yield to alternate hand,
might hold you shut in Teuthras' shallow stream,
rather than that you be free to hear another's soft whispers,
lying softly composed on a silent shore!
Not that you are not known to me, your good name proven,
but because in this region all love is feared.
So you will forgive me, if my little books
have brought you anything sad: it will be the fault of fear.
Ah, may I have no greater care than for a dear mother,
or any care of my life apart from you!
You alone are my home, you, Cynthia, alone my parents,
you all the seasons of my gladness.
Whether I come sad or, on the contrary, glad to my friends,
whatever I shall be, I will say, 'Cynthia was the cause.'
Only leave corrupting Baiae as soon as you can:
those shores will bring many a parting,
shores that have been enemies to chaste girls:
ah, perish the waters of Baiae, the reproach of love!

12. Why do you not cease to invent against me the charge of idleness,
that Cynthia keeps me lingering in Rome?
She is parted from my bed by as many miles
as the Hypanis is divided from the Venetian Eridanus;
nor does Cynthia nourish my accustomed loves with embrace,
nor sound sweet in my ear.
Once I was pleasing: at no time was it granted
to anyone that he could love with like faith.
We were the object of envy: has some god crushed me? or what
herb, gathered on Promethean ridges, divides us?
I am not what I was: a long journey changes girls.
How great a love has fled in a brief time!
Now for the first time I am forced to know the long nights
alone, and to be heavy to my own ears.
Happy is he who could weep before his present girl
(Love rejoices, somewhat sprinkled with tears),
or, if scorned, could change his ardours
(there are joys too in a servitude transferred).
But for me it is right neither to love another nor to leave her:
Cynthia was the first, Cynthia will be the end.

13. You, as you often do, will rejoice in my fall,
Gallus, that I lie empty, my love snatched away.
But I will not imitate your words, faithless one:
may no girl ever wish to deceive you, Gallus.
While your fame grows with deceived girls,
and, sure of yourself, you seek no delay in any love,
ruined for a certain one, you begin to grow pale
with slow cares, and, slipping, to fall at the first step.
This will be the penalty for the grief of those you scorned:
one girl will exact the wretched fates of many.
This common girl will check those loves of yours,
nor will you, ever seeking the new, be a friend.
I learned this not from evil rumour, nor taught by augur;
I saw it: can you, I beg, deny it with me as witness?
I saw you grow faint, bound about her whole neck,
and weep long, Gallus, with arms cast around her,
and long to lay down your life on the lips you craved,
and what after that, friend, my modesty conceals.
I could not pull your embraces apart:
so great was the maddened frenzy between you both.
Not so did the Taenarian god, mingled with Haemonian Enipeus,
press Salmoneus' daughter in willing love,
nor so did the burning love of Hercules feel
heavenly Hebe's first joys from the Oetaean pyres.
One day was able to outrun all lovers:
for she set beneath you no lukewarm torches,
nor let past disdains take their place,
nor will she: bound, your ardour will drive you on.
Nor is it strange, since she is next to Leda, worthy of Jove,
and more pleasing than Leda's offspring, one of three;
she would be more charming than Inachian heroines,
she could compel Jove himself to love by her words.
But since you are once for all to perish of love,
use it: you were worthy of no other threshold.
Since a new error has befallen you, may it be lucky;
and however many you wished, let her be your only one.

14. Though you lie at ease softly by the Tiber's wave
and drink Lesbian wines from Mentor's workmanship,
and now marvel at the swift skiffs running by
and now at the barges going slow on their tow-ropes;
and though the whole grove rear its planted woods aloft,
with as many trees as press upon Caucasus;
still these could not match my love:
Love does not know how to yield to great riches.
For whether she draws out longed-for rest with me,
or passes the whole day in easy love,
then the waters of Pactolus come beneath my roof,
and pearls are gathered beneath the Red Sea;
then my joys promise that kings will yield to me:
may they last, until the fates will have me perish!
For who rejoices in riches when Love is against him?
Let no rewards be mine with Venus gloomy!
She can break the great strength of heroes,
she can be a grief even to hard hearts:
she fears not to cross an Arabian threshold,
nor dreads, Tullus, to mount a purple couch,
and to toss the wretched youth all over his bed:
what ease bring silks with their varied weaves?
While she is present to me, appeased, I shall fear
no kingdoms, and I will scorn the gifts of Alcinous.

15. Often I feared much harsh treatment from your fickleness,
yet not this perfidy, Cynthia, before now.
See in how great a peril fortune snatches me away!
Yet you come slow to my fear;
and you can arrange yesterday's hair with your hands
and seek your beauty in long idleness,
and load your breast no less with Eastern gems,
as a fair girl who prepares to go to a new lover.
Not so was Calypso moved at the Ithacan's departure,
weeping once on the deserted seas:
many days she sat, mourning with unkempt hair,
speaking much to the unjust sea,
and though she would never see him again after this,
still she grieved, conscious of long happiness.
Not so did Hypsipyle, anxious at the winds carrying off
the son of Aeson, stand in her empty chamber:
Hypsipyle felt no loves after those,
once she wasted away in her Haemonian guest's love.
Evadne, borne high through the wretched fires,
died, the glory of Argive chastity.
Alphesiboea avenged her brothers for her husband,
and love broke the bonds of dear blood.
None of these could change your ways,
that you too might become a noble tale.
Cease now to recall your perjuries with words,
Cynthia, and forbear to stir the forgetful gods;
too bold, ah, you will grieve at my peril,
if by chance something harsher befall you!
Sooner shall deep rivers glide back to the sea,
and the year lead round its seasons reversed,
than the care for you be changed beneath my breast:
be whatever you will, you shall still not be a stranger to me.
Let not those eyes seem so cheap to you,
by which your perfidy has so often been trusted to me!
By these you used to swear, if you had lied in anything,
that they should fall from your hands into your lap:
and can you raise them against the great Sun,
and not tremble, conscious of the wickedness admitted?
Who forced you to grow pale with many colours
and to draw weeping from unwilling eyes?
By these I now perish, ready to warn lovers like me
to trust no flatteries as safe.

16. I, who once stood open to great triumphs,
a door vowed to Patrician Chastity,
whose threshold gilded chariots have thronged,
wet with the suppliant tears of captives,
now I, wounded by the nightly brawls of drunkards,
beaten by unworthy hands, often complain,
and there is no lack of shameful garlands hung on me,
and always torches lie, the marks of one shut out.
Nor can I ward off the shameful cries about my mistress,
given over, noble that I am, to obscene songs;
yet she is not recalled to spare her own good name,
to live the fouler for the luxury of the age.
Among these I am forced more grievously to bewail my complaints,
sadder for a suppliant's long night-watches.
He never lets my doorposts rest,
singing songs with clever blandishment:
'Door, crueller far than your own mistress,
why do you stand silent, closed to me with such hard doors?
Why do you never, unbarred, admit my love,
unknowing, unmoved, to return my stealthy prayers?
Will no end be granted to our grief,
and will shameful sleep be on a lukewarm threshold?
Midnight pities me, the sinking stars pity me as I lie,
and the cold breeze with its dawn frost.
O that my little voice, cast through a hollow chink,
might turn and strike the ears of my mistress!
Though she be more patient than Sicilian rock,
though she be harder than iron and steel,
still she will not be able to control her own eyes,
and a sigh will rise in unwilling tears.
Now she lies, leaning on another's lucky arm,
but my words fall to the night Zephyr.
But you alone, you the greatest cause of my grief,
door never won by my gifts,
you alone, never pitying human griefs,
answer me back with your silent hinges.
No wantonness of my tongue has wronged you;
such as an angry man is wont to say in bitter jest,
that you should let me, hoarse with so long a complaint,
keep an anxious vigil at the crossroads, delayed?
But for you I often drew off songs in fresh verse,
and, leaning on the steps, gave them pressing kisses.
How often, faithless one, did I turn before your posts,
and offer the vows I owed with hidden hands!'
This he says, and whatever you wretched lovers have known,
and drowns out the morning birds.
So now, by my mistress' vices and the weeping
of one always in love, I am torn by alternating reproach.

17. And rightly so, since I could flee my girl,
now I speak to the lonely halcyons.
Nor will Cassiope see my ship come safely,
and all my vows fall on a thankless shore.
Nay, even in your absence, Cynthia, the winds work for you:
see how the gale roars out its savage threats.
Will no calm come of a softened storm?
Will this little sand cover my dead body?
Yet turn your savage complaints to better:
let the night and the unjust shallows be punishment enough for you.
Or will you be able to demand back my fate with dry eyes,
and hold no bones of mine to your bosom?
Ah, let him perish, whoever first prepared the rafts and sails
and made his way over the unwilling deep!
Was it not easier to overcome my mistress' ways
(though hard, yet a rare girl she was),
than to behold these shores ringed with unknown woods,
and to seek the longed-for Tyndarids?
There, if some fates had buried my grief,
and the last stone stood with my love laid to rest,
she would have given her dear hair at my funeral,
and softly laid my bones on a tender rose;
she would have called my name over the final dust,
that the earth might lie on me with no weight.
But you, fair daughters of Doris of the sea,
spread the white sails with your lucky band:
if ever Love, gliding, has touched your waves,
spare a comrade on your gentle shores.

18. These places, surely, are deserted and silent for one who complains,
and the breeze of Zephyr possesses the empty grove.
Here I may bring out my hidden griefs unpunished,
if only the lonely rocks can keep faith.
From what beginning shall I first retrace your disdain, my Cynthia?
What cause of weeping, Cynthia, do you give me?
I, who but now was numbered among happy lovers,
now am forced to bear a mark in your love.
What have I so deserved? what crimes change you toward me?
Is a new girl the cause of your sadness?
So may you return to me, fickle one, as no other
has brought fair feet across my threshold.
Though this grief of mine owes you much that is harsh,
still my anger will not have come so savage
that I should be your frenzy always for cause, and your eyes,
from weeping, be made ugly with downcast tears.
Is it because I give few signs by a changed colour,
and no faith cries out in my face?
You will be witnesses, if a tree has any loves,
beech and the pine dear to the Arcadian god.
Ah, how often my words echo beneath your shadows,
and 'Cynthia' is written on the tender bark!
Ah, how many cares your wrong has borne me,
things known only to your silent doors!
I have grown used, timid, to endure all the haughty
commands, and not to complain of your deeds with sharp grief.
For this I am given the unbroken mountains and the cold cliff
and a hard rest on an untrodden path;
and whatever my complaints can tell,
I am forced to say to the shrill birds alone.
But whatever you are, let the woods echo 'Cynthia' to me,
and let the lonely rocks not be empty of your name.

19. I do not now, my Cynthia, fear the gloomy shades,
nor do I delay the fate owed to the final pyre;
but that my funeral might lack your love—
this fear is harder than the obsequies themselves.
Not so lightly has the boy clung to my eyes
that my dust should be free of love, forgotten.
There the hero, son of Phylacus, of his sweet wife
could not, in the dark places, be unmindful,
but, eager to touch his joys with phantom hands,
the Thessalian shade had come to his ancient home.
There, whatever I shall be, I will always be called your image:
great love crosses even the shores of fate.
There let the chorus of fair heroines come,
whom the Dardan spoil gave to the Argive men:
of whom none, Cynthia, will be more pleasing to me
than your beauty—and (so may just Earth allow it)
though the fates of long old age delay you,
your bones will still be dear to my tears.
Would that you, living, might feel this for my ashes!
Then death would not be bitter to me anywhere.
How I fear, Cynthia, that, scorning my tomb,
unjust Love may drag you from my dust,
and force you, unwilling, to dry the falling tears!
A steadfast girl is bent by constant threats.
So, while we may, let us be glad, we lovers, between us:
love is never long enough at any time.

20. This for the sake of your unbroken love, Gallus, we warn you,
that it may not slip from your idle mind:
often fortune meets the unwary lover:
so cruel was Ascanius to the Minyae.
You have a passion not below Hylas in looks, not unlike in name,
closest to Hylas, son of Theiodamas:
for him, whether you skim the rivers of the shadowy wood by raft,
or the wave of Anio wets your feet,
or you walk the edge of the Giants' shore,
or anywhere by the wandering hospitality of a stream,
always defend him from the eager rapine of the Nymphs
(no less is the love of the Ausonian Dryads);
lest it be yours, Gallus, to go forever to hard mountains
and cold rocks and untried lakes.
These the wretched Hercules, suffering wandering error on unknown shores,
had wept over for unconquered Ascanius.
For they say that once the Argo, sailing from the docks of Pagasa,
went far on its way from Phasis,
and, already gliding past the waves of Athamas' daughter,
brought its ship to the Mysian rocks.
Here the band of heroes, when it landed on the calm shores,
covered the soft beach with laid-out leaves.
But the comrade of the unconquered youth had gone further
to seek the scarce water of a secluded spring.
Two brothers pursued him, the offspring of Aquilo
(now Zetes flies above, now Calais),
striving to snatch kisses with hovering feet,
and to bear kisses in turn in alternating flight.
But he mocks them as they hang at his wing-tips
and wards off the winged ambush with a branch.
Now the race of Pandion's Orithyia gave way:
ah, grief! Hylas went on, went on to the Hamadryads.
Here beneath the peak of Mount Arganthus was Pege,
a pleasant home, moist, for the Thynian Nymphs,
over which hung dewy apples, owed to no care,
beneath the wild trees,
and round about, in the watered meadow, rose lilies,
white mingled with crimson poppies.
Now plucking these childishly with tender nail,
he preferred the flower to his appointed task,
and now, leaning unaware over the lovely waters,
he delays his straying with the charming reflections.
At last he prepares to draw the streams with lowered palms,
leaning on his right shoulder, drawing the full water.
When the Dryad girls, kindled by his beauty,
in wonder left off their accustomed dances
and drew him, slipping, gently through the yielding water,
then Hylas made a sound, his body snatched away.
To him from afar Alcides answers thrice, 'Hylas!' but to him
the breeze brings back the name from the farthest mountains.
By these warnings, O Gallus, you will guard your love,
lest you lose again your fair Hylas.

21. You who hasten to escape a shared fate,
soldier, wounded from the Etruscan ramparts,
why do you turn your swollen eyes at my groan?
I am the part of your warfare nearest you.
So, with you saved, may your parents be able to rejoice,
may this my sister learn what has happened from your tears:
that Gallus, snatched through the midst of Caesar's swords,
could not escape unknown hands;
and whatever scattered bones she may find
upon the Etruscan mountains, let her know these are mine.

22. What kind of man, and from what stock, who my household gods are, Tullus,
you ask, for the sake of our enduring friendship.
If the Perusine graves of our country are known to you,
the funerals of Italy in its hard times,
when Roman discord drove out its own citizens—
so, Etruscan dust, you are above all a grief to me,
you who suffered the cast-out limbs of my kinsman,
you who cover the bones of the wretch with no soil—
the Umbria next to it, touching the plains laid beneath,
bore me, fertile in its rich lands.

1. You ask why I write so often of love,
whence my soft book comes upon the lips.
Not Calliope, not Apollo sings these things to me.
The girl herself makes my talent.
Whether you bid her walk gleaming in Coan silk,
from this Coan gown the whole volume will come;
or if I have seen her loose hair stray over her brow,
she delights to go proud of her praised locks;
or if she has struck the lyre's song with ivory fingers,
I marvel how deftly her skilled hands press the strings;
or when she droops her eyes that crave sleep,
I, a poet, find a thousand new themes;
or when, stripped, she wrestles with me, her cloak snatched off,
then indeed we compose long Iliads;
or whatever she has done, or whatever she has said,
from nothing the greatest history is born.
But if the fates, Maecenas, had granted me only
the power to lead bands of heroes to arms,
I would not sing of the Titans, nor of Ossa piled
on Olympus, that Pelion might be a road to heaven,
nor ancient Thebes, nor Pergama, the fame of Homer,
nor that two straits met at Xerxes' command,
nor the first kingdoms of Remus, or the courage of lofty Carthage,
the threats of the Cimbri and the good deeds of Marius:
the wars and deeds of your Caesar I would recall, and you,
below great Caesar, would be my second care.
For whenever I sang of Mutina, or Philippi, the graves of civil war,
or the fleet-battles of the Sicilian rout,
the overthrown hearths of the ancient Etruscan race,
and the captured shores of Ptolemy's Pharos,
or when I sang of Egypt and the Nile, when, dragged into the city,
it went feeble with its seven captive streams,
or the necks of kings ringed with golden chains,
and the Actian beaks running along the Sacred Way;
my Muse would always weave you into those arms,
a head faithful both in war and in peace established:
as Theseus bears witness to the powers below, Achilles to those above,
the one to the son of Ixion, the other to the son of Menoetius.
. . .
But neither let Callimachus thunder of the Phlegraean strife
of Jupiter and Enceladus from his narrow breast,
nor does my heart suit me to found in hard verse
the name of Caesar among his Phrygian ancestors.
The sailor tells of winds, the ploughman of his oxen,
the soldier counts his wounds, the shepherd his sheep;
but I wage battles on a narrow bed:
let each man wear away the day in the art he can.
It is glory to die in love: a second glory, if it be granted
to enjoy one love alone: O may I enjoy my own love alone!
If I remember rightly, she is wont to blame fickle girls,
and for Helen's sake disapproves the whole Iliad.
Whether I must taste the cups of the stepmother Phaedra,
cups that would not harm her stepson,
or whether I must perish by Circe's herb, or whether
the Colchian boil her cauldron on Iolcian fires,
since one woman has plundered my senses,
from this house my funeral will be led.
Medicine heals all human griefs:
love alone loves no healer of its sickness.
Machaon healed the slow legs of Philoctetes,
Chiron, son of Phillyra, the eyes of Phoenix,
and the god of Epidaurus restored dead Androgeos
to his father's hearth with Cretan herbs,
and the Mysian youth, who had felt a wound from a Haemonian spear,
felt help from that very spear.
If anyone can take this fault from me,
he alone could put the apples in Tantalus' hand;
that same man could fill the casks with the maidens' urns,
that their tender necks be not burdened with endless water;
that same man could loose the arms of Prometheus from the Caucasian rock
and drive the bird from the middle of his breast.
Whenever, therefore, my fates demand back my life,
and I shall be a brief name upon a little marble stone,
Maecenas, the envied hope of our youth,
and the just glory of my life and death,
if by chance your road leads you near my tomb,
halt your British chariot at its carven yoke,
and, weeping, cast such words to the silent ashes:
'A hard girl was this poor man's doom.'

2. I was free, and meant to live with an empty bed;
but Love, peace once made, deceived me.
Why does this human beauty linger on earth?
Jupiter, I forgive your old thefts.
Golden is her hair, and long her hands, and tall her whole
body, and she walks as a sister even worthy of Jove,
or as when Pallas paces toward the Dulichian altars,
her breast covered by the snaky Gorgon's locks;
as was the heroine Ischomache, of Lapith stock,
a welcome prey to the Centaurs in the midst of the wine;
Mercury too is said, by the waters of Boebeis,
to have laid his side beside virgin Brimo.
Yield now, goddesses, whom the shepherd once saw
lay aside their tunics on the Idaean peaks!
Would that old age might not wish to change this beauty,
even if she should live the ages of the Cumaean prophetess!

3. 'You who said that nothing could now harm you,
you are caught fast, that spirit of yours has fallen!
Scarcely can you, poor wretch, rest for a single month,
and already there will be another shameful book about you.'
I used to ask whether a fish could live on dry sand
and the fierce boar, unused, in the sea;
or whether I could keep watch over stern studies:
any love is deferred, never removed.
It was not so much her face that took me, however fair
(let lilies be no whiter than my mistress;
as Maeotic snow vies with Iberian vermilion,
and as rose-petals float in pure milk),
nor her hair flowing in its way down her smooth neck,
nor her eyes, twin torches, our stars,
nor if some girl shines in Arabian silk
(I am no flattering lover for nothing):
so much as how beautifully she dances when the wine is set out,
as when Ariadne led the bands chanting euhoe,
and how, when she tries songs with the Aeolian quill,
learned to play matched with the Aganippean lyre;
and when she sets her writings beside ancient Corinna's,
poems that no one thinks equal to her own.
Did bright Love at your birth, my life, in your first days,
sneeze a clear omen over you?
The gods gave you these heavenly gifts,
nor think your mother chanced to give them.
No, no, such gifts are not of human birth:
ten months did not bring forth these blessings.
You alone are born the glory of Roman girls:
the first Roman girl, you will lie down with Jove,
nor will you ever visit human beds with us;
since Helen, this beauty returns to earth a second time.
Why should I marvel now if our youth burns for her?
It would have been fairer, Troy, for you to perish for her.
Once I marvelled that a girl was the cause of so great a war
at Pergama, of Europe and Asia:
now, Paris, you were wise, and you, Menelaus, were too,
you because you demanded, you because you were slow.
A face indeed worthy that even Achilles should die for it;
even Priam should approve it as the cause of war.
If anyone wishes to surpass the old paintings in fame,
let him set my mistress as a model in his art:
whether he shows her to the West or shows her to the East,
she will set on fire both East and West.
Within these limits at least let me now be held! Or, if any
keener love come to me, a second, that I may die!
And just as at first the bull refuses the plough,
then, the yoke grown familiar, comes gentle to the fields,
so at first fierce young men quail in love,
then, tamed, they bear thereafter the fair and the unfair alike.
The prophet Melampus endured shameful chains,
known to have stolen the cattle of Iphiclus;
whom no gain, but rather fair Pero compelled,
soon to be the bride of the house of Amythaon.

4. First you must complain of your mistress' many faults,
often ask something, often go away rebuffed,
and often gnaw your undeserving nails with your teeth,
and in anger stamp your faltering foot with a sound!
In vain were the perfumes poured on my hair,
and my foot moved with measured, lingering step.
Here no herb avails, no nocturnal Colchian,
no boiled herbs of Perimede's hand;
for to what false prophet am I not the reward?
What old woman does not turn my dreams ten times?
For where we discern neither causes nor open blows,
yet whence so many evils come is a hidden way;
this sick man needs no doctors, no soft beds,
no season of weather, no breeze harms him;
he walks—and suddenly his friends marvel at his funeral!
So unguarded is whatever is held to be love.
If I have any enemy, let him love girls:
let him rejoice in a boy, if anyone is my friend.
You go down a safe stream in a calm boat:
how can the wave of so small a shore harm you?
The one often changes his heart at a single word,
the other will scarcely soften even with one's own blood.

5. Is this true, that you are talked of through all Rome, Cynthia,
and live by no unknown wantonness?
Did I deserve to hope for this? You will pay me the penalty, faithless one;
and for me too, Cynthia, some wind will blow.
Yet I shall find one among the many deceivers
who will wish to become famous by my song,
nor will insult me with manners so harsh, and will
gall you: alas, too late will you weep, loved so long.
Now my anger is fresh, now is the time to depart:
if the grief is gone, believe me, love will return.
Not so do the Carpathian waves shift with the North winds,
nor does the black cloud turn with the doubtful South,
as easily are angry lovers changed by a word:
while you may, draw your neck from the unjust yoke.
And you will grieve, not a little, but on the first night;
every evil in love, if you endure it, is light.
But you, by the sweet laws of mistress Juno,
spare yourself, my life, lest your own spirit harm you.
Not only does the bull strike his foe with hooked horns,
but even the wounded sheep fights back against its attacker.
I will not tear the clothes from your perjured body,
nor will my anger break your barred doors,
nor will I, enraged, dare to pull your braided hair,
nor hurt you with hard thumbs:
let some boor seek such shameful battles,
whose head no ivy has wreathed.
So I will write what no age of yours can erase,
'Cynthia, mighty in beauty; Cynthia, light in words.'
Believe me, though you scorn the murmurs of rumour,
this verse, Cynthia, will turn you pale.

6. The house of Lais of Ephyre was not so crowded,
at whose doors all Greece lay;
Menander's Thais once had no such throng,
in whom the people of Erichthonius made sport;
nor Phryne, made rich by so many men,
she who could have rebuilt ruined Thebes.
Nay, you often feign false kinsmen for yourself,
nor are there lacking those who may kiss you by right.
The painted faces of young men wound me, their names wound me,
the tender boy in his cradle and without speech wounds me;
it wounds me if your mother gives you many kisses,
me your sister, and the friend who sleeps beside you:
all things wound me: I am timid (forgive my fear)
and, wretched, I suspect a man is in a woman's tunic.
By these faults, as the story goes, they once came to battle,
by these beginnings you see the Trojan funerals;
the same harsh madness bade the Centaurs
shatter their cups against Pirithous.
Why should I seek Greek examples? You, the author of crime,
nursed on the hard milk of the she-wolf, Romulus:
you taught the rape of the chaste Sabines to go unpunished:
through you Love now dares anything at Rome.
Happy the wife of Admetus and the marriage-bed of Ulysses,
and whatever woman loves her husband's threshold!
What need to have built temples to Chastity for girls,
if any bride is allowed to be anything she likes?
The hand that first painted obscene pictures
and set foul sights in a chaste house,
that hand corrupted the innocent eyes of girls
and would not leave them ignorant of its own wickedness.
Ah, let him groan beneath the earth who brought forth by his art
things shameful, hidden under silent delight!
Not with such figures did men once adorn their homes:
then the wall was painted with no crime.
But not undeservedly! The spider has veiled the shrine
and evil grass overruns the deserted gods.
What guardians, then, what thresholds shall I set for you,
which no hostile foot may ever cross?
For stern watching is of no use against the unwilling:
she who is ashamed to sin, Cynthia, is safe enough.
No wife will ever lead me astray, no mistress ever:
you will always be my mistress, always my wife.

7. Cynthia surely rejoiced that the law was repealed,
at whose proclamation we both wept long ago,
lest it should part us: though Jupiter himself
cannot divide two lovers against their will.
'But Caesar is great.' Yet Caesar is great in arms:
conquered nations are worth nothing in love.
For I would sooner suffer this head to leave my neck
than I could waste the wedding torches at a bride's whim,
or pass, a husband, by your closed threshold,
looking back, betrayed, with wet eyes.
Ah, what songs of sleep my flute would then sing you,
a flute sadder than the funeral trumpet!
Whence should I furnish sons for Parthian triumphs?
No soldier will come of my blood.
But if I followed the true camp of my girl,
not great enough for me would Castor's horse ride.
For from this my glory has earned so great a name,
a glory carried to the wintry Borysthenians.
You alone please me: may I please you, Cynthia, alone:
this love will be worth more than my ancestral name.

8. The girl long dear to me is now being snatched away:
and you, friend, forbid me to shed tears?
No enmities are bitter except love's:
butcher me myself, I shall be a gentler foe.
Can I look at her laid on another's arm?
Will she not be called mine, who just now was called mine?
All things change: surely loves change:
you are conquered or you conquer, this is the wheel of love.
Great leaders often, great tyrants have fallen,
and Thebes had stood, and lofty Troy once was.
What great gifts I gave, what songs I made!
Yet she, iron-hearted, never said 'I love.'
Was I then too rash for so many years,
shameless one, that I bore you and your house?
Did I ever seem free to you? Or will you forever
hurl proud words upon my head?
So, then, will you die in your first youth, Propertius?
But die; let her rejoice in your destruction!
Let her torment my shade, hound my ghost,
insult my pyre, and trample my bones!
What? Did not Boeotian Haemon fall at Antigone's tomb,
his side wounded by his own sword,
and mingle his bones with the wretched girl's,
without whom he would not go to his Theban home?
But you will not escape: you must die with me;
from this same blade let the blood of both drip.
Though this death will be dishonourable to me:
a dishonourable death indeed, yet you shall die.
He too, Achilles, deserted when his wife was snatched away,
let his arms lie idle in his tent.
He had seen the Achaeans laid low in flight on the shore,
and the Dorian camp ablaze with Hector's torch;
he had seen Patroclus, disfigured on the heaped sand,
stretched out, his hair scattered in his blood,
enduring all for the sake of fair Briseis:
so great a grief rages over love snatched away.
But after the captive was given back, a late atonement,
he dragged that brave Hector behind his Haemonian steeds.
Since I am far inferior both in mother and in arms,

9. That which he now is, I have often been: but perhaps in an hour
another, this very one cast off, will be dearer.
Penelope could live untouched for twice ten years,
a woman worthy of so many suitors;
she could defer marriage by false Minerva,
undoing by night the work of day with a trick;
and though she never hoped to see Ulysses,
by waiting for him she stayed and became an old woman.
Briseis too, embracing the lifeless Achilles,
beat her white face with maddened hand;
and the captive, mourning, washed her bloody lord,
laid out by the yellow shallows of Simois,
and fouled her hair, and lifted the body of great Achilles
and his vast bones in her small hand;
when neither Peleus was near you nor your sea-blue mother,
nor Scyrian Deidamia in her widowed bed.
Then, therefore, Greece rejoiced in true brides,
then there was chaste honour even amid arms.
But you could not be empty for a single night,
impious one, could not stay alone for a single day!
Nay, you drank cups together with much laughter:
perhaps too there were evil words about me.
He too is sought, who first deserted you before:
may the gods grant you enjoy the man who caught you!
Were these the vows I undertook for your safety,
when the Stygian waters were already gaining this head,
and we friends stood weeping around your bed?
Where was he then, by the gods, faithless one, and who was he?
What if I were kept a soldier among the distant Indians,
or if my ship stood in the Ocean?
But for you it is easy to compose words and deceits:
this one work woman has always learned.
Not so do the Syrtes shift with the uncertain breeze,
nor leaves so trembled by the wintry South,
as swiftly a pact in a woman's anger breaks,
whether the cause be grave or the cause be light.
Now, since this resolve has pleased you, I shall yield:
bring out, I pray, boys, your sharper darts,
vie to pierce me, and free me from this life!
My blood will be your greatest prize.
The stars are witnesses, and the morning frost,
and the door opened stealthily to me, poor wretch,
that nothing in life was ever more dear to me than you:
now too it will be so, though you are my enemy, nothing.
Nor will any mistress set foot on my bed:
I shall be alone, since it is not allowed to be yours.
And would that, if I have led pious years,
that man might turn to stone in the midst of love!
. . .
The Theban leaders fell beneath dread arms, not for kingdoms more,
not without their mother between them,
than I, if I might fight with my girl between us,
would not flee to undergo death by your death.

10. But it is time to range Helicon with other dances,
and time now to give the field to the Haemonian horse.
Now I would gladly recall the squadrons brave in battle
and tell of the Roman camp of my leader.
But if my strength fails, surely the daring
will be praise: in great things even to have wished is enough.
Let first youth sing of Venus, the last of tumults:
I will sing of wars, since my girl has been written.
Now I wish to go forward graver, with downcast brow,
now my Muse teaches me another lyre.
Rise, soul, from the lowly; now, my song, take up strength;
Pierides, now there will be need of a mighty voice.
Now the Euphrates denies that the Parthian horseman looks behind
his back, and grieves to have detained the Crassi:
nay, India, Augustus, gives its neck to your triumph,
and the house of untouched Arabia trembles before you;
and if any land withdraws itself to the farthest shores,
let it later, captured, feel your hands!
This camp I will follow; by singing your camp
I shall be a great prophet: may the fates keep this day for me!
But where one cannot touch the head of the great standards,
the garland is laid here before its lowest feet;
so we now, unable to climb the song of praise,
give cheap incense at poor rites.
Not yet do my songs know the Ascraean springs,
but Love has only washed them in the stream of Permessus.

11. Let others write of you, or you may stay unknown:
let him praise you who sows seed in barren soil.
All your gifts, believe me, the black day of your last funeral
will carry off with you upon one bier;
and the traveller will pass by your bones in scorn,
nor will he say, 'This ash was once a learned girl.'

12. Whoever he was, who first painted Love as a boy,
do you not think he had wondrous hands?
He first saw that lovers live without sense,
and that great goods perish through light cares.
The same man not in vain added windy wings,
and made the god fly from the human heart:
for we are tossed on alternating waves,
and our breeze stays in no place.
And rightly his hand is armed with barbed arrows,
and the Cretan quiver hangs from either shoulder:
for he strikes before we, safe, discern the foe,
nor does anyone leave that wound unharmed.
In me the darts remain, the boyish image remains:
but surely he has lost his wings;
for, alas, he never flies away from my breast,
and wages constant war in my blood.
What pleasure is it to you to dwell in dried-up marrow?
If you have shame, hurl your darts elsewhere!
It were better to try the untouched with that poison:
it is not I, but my thin shade that is beaten.
For if you destroy it, who will there be to sing such things,
(this my light Muse is your great glory),
who would sing the head and the fingers and the dark eyes of the girl,

13. Not with so many Persian arrows are Etruscan
shafts armed as Love has fixed in my breast.
He forbade me to scorn the slender Muses,
and bade me dwell so in the Ascraean grove,
not that the Pierian oaks should follow my words,
or that I could lead the beasts down the Ismarian vale,
but rather that Cynthia should be astounded by my verse:
then would I be more famous in art than Inachian Linus.
I am not so great an admirer of mere noble beauty,
nor of a woman who boasts illustrious ancestors:
let it delight me to have read in the lap of a learned girl,
and to have proved my writings to pure ears.
When these things have befallen, farewell, confused tale
of the crowd: for with my mistress as judge I shall be safe.
And if she happens to turn kind ears toward peace,
then I can endure the enmity of Jove.

13b. Whenever, therefore, death shall close my eyes,
learn the rites of my funeral that you may keep.
Let not my procession then range with long display,
nor let the trumpet be the empty lament of my death;
nor let a couch be spread for me on an ivory frame,
nor let my death rest on a couch of Attalus.
Let the row of perfume-bearing dishes be absent, let there be
the small obsequies of a plebeian funeral.
My procession is great enough, if there be three little books,
which I shall bear as greatest gifts to Persephone.
But you, your breast bared and torn, will follow,
nor will you grow weary of calling my name,
and you will place last kisses on my cold lips,
when the onyx full of Syrian gift is given.
Then, when the fire set beneath has made me ashes,
let a tiny urn receive my shade,
and let a laurel be set above the small tomb,
to shade with its shadow the place of my spent funeral,
and let there be two verses: WHO NOW LIES HERE, GRIM DUST,
WAS ONCE THE SLAVE OF A SINGLE LOVE.
Nor will the fame of my grave grow less known
than the bloody tomb of the Phthian hero.
You too, if ever you come to your fate, remember,
come white-haired by this road to the mindful stones.
Meanwhile take care not to scorn me when buried:
the knowing earth has no small sense of truth.
And would that one of the Three Sisters had bidden me
lay down my life in my first cradle!
For why should the breath be kept for so doubtful an hour?
Nestor's ash was seen after three generations:
yet if some Gallic soldier on the Trojan ramparts
had shortened for him the fate of long old age,
he would not have seen the body of Antilochus buried,
nor said, 'O death, why do you come to me so late?'
Yet you will sometimes weep for your lost friend:
it is right to love forever those who have passed.
Witness he whom the hard boar once struck, white Adonis,
as he hunted on the Idalian height,
lay handsome in those marshes; thither
you, Venus, are said to have gone with hair flowing loose.
But in vain, Cynthia, will you call back my silent shade:

14. Not so did the son of Atreus rejoice in the Dardan triumph,
when the great wealth of Laomedon fell;
nor was Ulysses so glad when his wandering was done,
when he touched the shores of dear Dulichia;
nor Electra so, when she beheld Orestes safe,
whose false bones, holding, the sister had wept;
nor did the daughter of Minos so see Theseus unharmed,
when with the thread he guided his Daedalian path;
as much joy as I have gathered in the past night:
I shall be immortal, if there be another such.
But while I went a suppliant with bowed neck,
I was said to be cheaper than a dry pool.
Now she no longer seeks to set unjust disdains against me,
nor can she sit slow while I weep.
And would that this terms had not been known to me so late!
Now medicine is given to ashes.
The path shone before my blind feet:
for surely no one in mad love sees.
This I have felt to profit more: scorn them, lovers!
So today she will come who refused yesterday.
Others knocked in vain and called the mistress:
with me the slow girl had laid her head.
This is a victory dearer to me than the conquered Parthians,
these will be my spoils, my kings, my chariots.
Great gifts I will fix on your column, Cytherea,
and such a song will be beneath my name:
THESE SPOILS I, PROPERTIUS, PLACE BEFORE YOUR SHRINE, GODDESS,
A LOVER RECEIVED THROUGH THE WHOLE NIGHT.
Now it lies with you, my light, whether my ship comes to harbour
saved, or settles laden in the midst of the shallows.
But if by some fault you change toward me,
may I lie dead before your porch!

15. O happy me! O night bright for me! and O you,
little couch made blessed by my delights!
How many words we spoke with the lamp set near,
and what a struggle there was when the light was removed!
For now she wrestled with me, her breasts bared,
now, covered by her tunic, she made delay.
She opened my eyes that had slipped in sleep
with her own mouth and said, 'So, sluggard, you lie?'
How with varied embrace we change our arms! How long
my kisses lingered on your lips!
It does not please to spoil Venus with blind motion:
if you do not know it, the eyes are the leaders in love.
Paris himself is said to have perished for the naked Spartan,
when she rose from Menelaus' chamber;
naked too Endymion is said to have caught Phoebus' sister
and lain with the naked goddess.
But if, persisting in your purpose, you lie clothed,
you will feel my hands with your garment torn:
nay, even, if anger carries me further,
you will show your mother your bruised arms.
Not yet do drooping breasts forbid you to play:
let her see to that who is already ashamed to have borne a child.
While the fates allow us, let us sate our eyes with love:
a long night comes for you, and a day that will not return.
And would that you wished to bind us so, clinging, with a chain,
that no day might ever loose it!
Let the doves joined in love be your example,
male and female, a whole marriage.
He errs who seeks an end to mad love:
true love knows no measure to keep.
Sooner shall the earth deceive the ploughman with false birth,
and the Sun more quickly drive black horses,
and the rivers begin to call back their waters to their source,
and the fish be dry in a parched whirlpool,
than I could transfer my griefs to another:
hers I shall be living, hers I shall be dead.
But if she will grant me such nights with her,
even a year of life will be long.
If she gives many, I shall become immortal in them:
in a single night anyone can be even a god.
If all men longed to run such a life,
and to lie with limbs heavy with much wine,
there would be no cruel sword nor warship,
nor would the Actian sea toss our bones,
nor would Rome, so often besieged round about by her own triumphs,
be weary of loosing her hair in mourning.
This at least posterity will rightly be able to praise:
our cups have wronged no gods.
Only you, while it is light, do not abandon the fruit of life!
If you give all your kisses, you will give too few.
And as the leaves leave the withering garlands,
which you see scattered everywhere, floating in the baskets,
so for us, who now breathe high as lovers,
perhaps tomorrow's day will shut up our fate.

16. The praetor has just come, Cynthia, from the Illyrian lands,
the greatest prey for you, the greatest care for me.
Could he not have laid down his life on the Ceraunian rock?
Ah, Neptune, what gifts I would give you!
Now without me the banquets are held at a full table,
now without me the door stands open all night.
So, if you are wise, do not abandon the harvest offered
and fleece the stupid sheep of its full coat;
then, when, his gift spent, he is left a pauper,
bid him sail again to other Illyrias!
Cynthia does not follow the fasces nor care for honours,
she always weighs the purse of her lovers.
But you now, Venus, O help my grief,
that he may burst his limbs with endless lusts!
So anyone buys love with gifts?
Jupiter, the girl perishes for an unworthy price.
She always sends me to seek pearls in the Ocean,
and bids me bring gifts from Tyre itself.
And would that no one at Rome were rich, and the leader himself
could dwell in a hut of straw!
Never would mistresses be for sale to a gift,
and the same girl would grow grey in one house;
never would you lie apart for seven nights,
your white arms flung round so foul a man,
not because I have sinned (I call you to witness), but because
fickleness has always been the friend of fair women.
The barbarian stirs his loins with his ankles shut tight,
and suddenly, lucky, he now holds my kingdom!
See what Eriphyle found by bitter gifts,
and with what evils the bride Creusa burned.
Will no wrong soothe my weeping?
Or does this grief not know how to be absent from your vices?
So many days have now gone, when neither the care of the theatre
nor of the Campus has touched me, nor does my table please.
But surely let her be ashamed, ashamed! unless perhaps, as they say,
shameful love is wont to have deaf ears.
Behold the leader, who lately filled with empty din
the Actian seas with his doomed soldiers:
shameful love bade him turn his keels in flight
and seek refuge at the world's edge.
This is Caesar's virtue and Caesar's glory:
with the hand by which he conquered, he laid up his arms.
But whatever garments he gave you, whatever emeralds,
or topaz with its golden light,
may I see the swift gales carry these to nothing:
may they become, I wish, earth to you, water to you.
Not always does serene Jupiter laugh at perjured lovers
and neglect their prayers with deaf ear.
You have seen the thunder run across the whole sky,
and the lightning leap down from its ethereal home:
this the Pleiades do not, nor watery Orion,
nor does the wrath of the bolt fall thus from nothing;
then is he wont to punish perjured girls,
since, deceived, the god himself once wept.
So let not a Sidonian garment be worth so much to you
that you fear, whenever the South wind is cloudy.

17. To break the promised night, to lead the lover on with promises,
this is to have hands stained with blood!
Of these I am the prophet, whenever, deserted, I have spent
bitter nights, tossing on both sides of the bed.
Whether you are moved by the lot of Tantalus at the streams,
that the water mocks the thirst of his parched mouth;
or whether you wonder at the labours of Sisyphus,
how hard it is to roll the weight up the whole mountain;
nothing on earth lives harder than a lover,
nor, if you are wise, would you wish to be anything less.
He whom envy lately bore as happy, marvelling,
now I am scarcely admitted even on the tenth day.
Now it pleases me, impious one, to lay my body on the hard rock,
and to take the ground poison into my hands;
nor may I rest in the crossroads under the dry moon,
or send words through the chinks of doors.
Yet however this may be, I will beware of changing my mistress:
then she will weep, when she feels that there is faith in me.

18a. Constant complaints have bred hatred in many:
often a woman is broken by a silent man.
If you have seen anything, always deny you have seen it!
Or if anything has chanced to grieve her, deny that you grieve!

18b. What if my age were growing white with grey years,
and a languid wrinkle made my cheeks furrowed?
Yet Aurora, not scorning the old age of Tithonus,
did not let him lie deserted in her Eastern home:
him often, as she departed, she cherished in her arms
before she diligently washed the harnessed horses;
when, embracing him, she rested near the Indians,
she complained that the days returned too soon;
she, mounting her chariot, called the gods unjust,
and did her duty to the lands unwilling.
For her the joys of living old Tithonus were greater
than was her heavy grief at Memnon lost.
It did not shame such a girl to sleep with an old man
and so often to give kisses to white hair.
But you hate me even young, faithless one, though you yourself
will be a bent old woman in no long day.
Nay, I lessen my care, since often Cupid
is wont to be ill to him to whom he was good before.

18c. Now even, madwoman, do you imitate the painted Britons,
and sport with your head dyed in foreign sheen?
As nature gave it, so every figure is right:
the Belgian colour is foul on a Roman face.
May many evils befall that girl beneath the earth
who foolishly, lying, changes her own hair!
Take it off: surely you can seem fair to me,
you are fair enough for me, if only you come often.
Or if some girl has dyed her temples with blue tint,
is a blue beauty therefore good?
Since you have neither brother nor any son,
let me be your brother, and let me be your only son.
Let your own bed always be your guardian,
nor wish to sit with too adorned a brow.
I will believe rumour as it tells: do not give it cause:
rumour leaps across both land and seas.

19. Although you depart from Rome against my will, Cynthia,
I rejoice that you will dwell in remote fields without me.
There will be no young corrupter in the chaste fields,
who would not let you be virtuous with his flatteries;
no brawl will arise before your windows,
nor will sleep be bitter to you when called upon.
You will be alone and gaze alone, Cynthia, at the mountains
and the flock and the bounds of a poor farmer.
There no games can corrupt you,
nor shrines, the greatest cause of your sins.
There you will continually watch the bulls ploughing,
and the vine lay aside its tresses to the learned pruning-hook;
and there you will bring scant incense to the rough chapel,
where the rustic kid falls before the hearths;
at once you will imitate the dances with bare leg;
let all things only be safe from a stranger.
I myself will hunt: now already it pleases me
to take up the rites of Diana and lay aside the vows of Venus.
I will begin to chase wild beasts and hang the horns
on the pine, and myself to urge on the bold dogs;
not, however, that I would dare to attack vast lions
or go swift to close quarters with the field-boars.
Let this then be my soft daring, to catch
gentle hares and pierce the bird with the fitted reed,
where Clitumnus covers his fair streams with his grove,
and the wave washes the snowy oxen.
Whenever you attempt anything, my life, remember
that I will come to you within a few dawns.
Here neither the lonely woods can turn me away,
nor the wandering streams poured down the mossy ridges,
from changing your name on my unceasing tongue:
no one would wish not to have harmed the absent.

20. Why do you weep more grievously than Briseis snatched away? why do you weep,
anxious, more sadly than captive Andromache?
or why, madwoman, do you weary the gods about my treachery?
Why do you complain that my faith has fallen so?
Not so loudly does the Attic bird, deadly in nocturnal complaint,
cry amid the Cecropian leaves,
nor so much does Niobe, proud over twice-six graves,
flow down weeping from anxious Sipylus.
Though they bind my arms with brazen knots,
though your limbs be hidden in the house of Danae,
for you I will break even the brazen chains, my life,
and leap across the iron house of Danae.
Whatever is said of you, it is said to my deaf ears:
only do not doubt my steadfastness.
I swear to you by my mother's bones and my father's bones
(if I lie, alas, may both ashes be heavy on me!)
that I will remain yours, my life, to the final darkness:
one faith, one day, will carry us both off.
But if neither your name nor your beauty held me,
your gentle servitude could hold me.
Now the seventh circle of the full moon is drawn down,
since no crossroads are silent about me and you:
meanwhile your door has sometimes been soft to me,
sometimes the freedom of your bed has been granted.
Nor was any night bought for me with blessed gifts:
whatever I was, this was the great grace of your heart.
When so many sought you, you alone sought me:
can I be unmindful of your nature?
Then may the tragic Furies torment me, and may you
condemn me, Aeacus, in the infernal judgment,
and may my punishment wander among the birds of Tityus,
and may I bear the rocks in Sisyphus' toil!
Nor do you sue me with suppliant tablets:
my last faith will be such as my first.
This is my perpetual law, that I, alone among lovers,
neither quickly cease nor rashly begin.

21. Ah, how much Panthus' page has feigned to you about me,
so much may Venus not be a friend to that Panthus!
But already I seem to you a truer prophet than Dodona.
That handsome lover of yours has a wife!
So many nights have perished: is there no shame? Look, he sings
free: you, too credulous, lie alone.
And now you are talk between them, and he, proud,
says that he was often at home against his will.
May I perish, if anything but glory is sought
from you: this husband has these praises.
So did the guest Jason once deceive the Colchian:
she was cast out of the house (for Creusa held it).
So was Calypso mocked by the Dulichian youth:
she saw her lover spread his sails.
Ah, too easy girls, to lend your ears,
learn, deserted ones, not to be rashly kind!
For this one too, who remains, another has long been sought:
experienced in the first, foolish, you can beware.
We in whatever place, we at every time are with you,
whether sick alike or in health.

22a. You know that yesterday many girls pleased me alike;
you know, Demophoon, that many ills come to me.
No crossroads are roamed in vain by my feet;
O theatres too much born for my ruin,
whether someone parts her white arms with a soft gesture,
or sings varied measures with her mouth!
Meanwhile my eyes seek a wound for themselves,
if some fair girl sits with uncovered breast,
or if wandering locks stray on pure brows,
which an Indian gem holds at the top of the head.
If by chance she has harshly refused me anything with her look,
cold sweat fell from all my brow.
You ask, Demophoon, why I am so weak toward all?
What you ask, 'why,' no love has.
Why does someone slash his arms with sacred knives
and cut himself to the Phrygian's frenzied measures?
To each created thing nature has given a fault:
to me fortune has given always to love something.
Though the fate of Thamyras the singer follow me,
I will never, envious one, be blind to fair women.
But if I seem to you thin, wasted in my limbs,
you are deceived: Venus is never won by labour.
You may inquire: often a girl has proved
my service strong the whole night through.
Jupiter rested twin Bears for Alcmene,
and the sky was twice by night without its king;
yet not therefore did he come languid to his thunderbolts:
no love itself takes away its own strength.
What? When Achilles went from the embrace of Briseis,
did the Phrygians flee the Thessalian darts the less?
What? When fierce Hector rose from Andromache's bed,
did the Mycenaean ships not fear war?
The one or the other could destroy fleets or walls:
here I am the son of Peleus, here I the fierce Hector.
See how in the sky now the sun, now the moon serves:
so for me too one girl is too little.
Let one hold and cherish me with eager arms,
if the other ever leaves me no room;
or if by chance she is made angry at my servant,
let her know there is another who wishes to be mine!
For two cables better guard a ship,
and the anxious mother more safely rears twins.

22b. Or if you are hard, refuse: but if you are not hard, come!
What good is it to set these words nowhere?
This one grief is keen of all to a lover,
if some girl whom he hopes for suddenly refuses to come.
How many sighs turn him all over his bed,
when she herself forbids him to receive one who has not come?
And again, asking, he wearies the boy with what he has heard,
bidding him seek the fates he fears to know.

23. He for whom the path of the untaught crowd had to be shunned,
now the water sought from the very pool is sweet to me.
Does any freeborn man give gifts to another's slave,
that he may carry the promised words to his mistress?
And asks so often, 'What portico now
covers her?' and 'How does she move her feet on the Campus?'
Then, when you have endured what fame calls the labours
of Hercules, so that she writes, 'Have you any gift?',
that you may see the face of a bitter guardian,
and, caught, often hide in a filthy hut?
How dearly the night turns once in a whole year!
Ah, let them perish, whom a closed door pleases!
On the other hand, she who goes free with cloak thrown back,
hedged by no fear of guardians, pleases?
For whom the Sacred Way is often worn by a dirty shoe,
nor does she allow delay, if anyone wishes to approach;
she will never put it off, nor, prattling, demand what
the father, tied up, often weeps to have given,
nor will she say, 'I am afraid, hasten now to rise, I beg:
unhappy me, today my man comes from the country.'
And those whom the Euphrates and those whom the Orontes have sent me,
let them help me: I would not have chaste thefts of the bed;
since no freedom now remains to any lover:
no one will be free, if anyone wishes to love.

24a. 'Do you speak, when you are already a tale in a famous book
and your Cynthia is read throughout the whole forum?'
For whom would not sweat sprinkle his temples at these words?
Either honest shame, or a love that must be kept silent.
But if Cynthia breathed so easy upon us,
I would not be called the head of wantonness,
nor be led, infamous, through the whole city,
and though I burned, I would put words off under a false name.
So let it not be strange to you that I seek cheap girls:
they defame less: is the reason light to you?
. . .
And now she desires fans of the proud peacock's tail
and to have a cool ball of hard crystal in her hands,
and she demands, when I am angry, the ivory dice,
and the cheap gifts that gleam on the Sacred Way.
Ah, let me perish, if those expenses move me, but it
shames me now to be a jest to a deceiving mistress!

24b. Was this above all what you bade me rejoice in?
Are you not ashamed, so fair, to be so fickle?
Not one or two nights yet have been spent in love,
and already I am said to be heavy in your bed.
Lately you praised me and read my songs:
has that love of yours turned its wings so quickly?
Let him contend with me in talent, let him contend in art,
first of all let him learn to love in one house:
if it pleases you, let him fight the Lernaean hydra
and bring you apples from the Hesperian dragon,
let him gladly drink foul poisons and, shipwrecked, the waves,
and never refuse to be wretched for your sake:
(would that you might prove these labours in me, my life!)
soon that bold one will be among the timid for you,
who now comes by tossing himself into swollen honour:
next year will be your parting.
But me no whole age of the Sibyl will change,
nor the toil of Alcides, nor that black day.
You will gather my bones and say, 'Are these your bones,
Propertius? Alas, you were faithful to me,
faithful you were, alas, though not noble in ancestral
blood, and though you were not so rich.'
I will endure anything, no wrong ever changes me:
to bear a fair girl I think no burden.
I believe not a few have perished for that beauty,
I believe, but that many have not had faith.
For a short space Theseus loved the daughter of Minos,
Demophoon Phyllis, each a wicked guest.
Now Medea is known to you by the Jasonian keel
and lately left alone by the man she saved.
She is hard who feigns a pretended love to many,
and can make herself ready for more than one.
Do not compare me with the noble, do not with the blessed:
scarcely comes one who would gather my bones on my last day.
These I will be to you: but rather, I pray, that you
beat your bare breast with hair let down for me.

25. Only one, the fairest, born to my grief,
since my lot shuts out 'come often,'
that beauty of yours will become most famous in my little books,
by your leave, Calvus, by your peace, Catullus.
The aged soldier lies apart, his arms laid down,
and the aged oxen refuse to draw the ploughs,
and the rotting ship rests on the empty sand,
and the old war-shield hangs idle in the temple:
but no old age will lead me from your love,
whether I shall be Tithonus or Nestor.
Was it not better to serve a hard tyrant
and groan in your bull, cruel Perillus?
It were better to harden at the Gorgon's face,
even if we suffered the Caucasian birds.
Yet still I will resist. The iron blade is worn by rust,
and the flint often by a little water:
but love is worn away by no fault of the mistress, which
remains and endures threats with undeserving ear.
Unasked, scorned, he begs, and, wronged, confesses
that he has sinned, and himself returns with unwilling feet.
You too, who in full love assume disdain,
credulous one, no woman has weight for long.
Does anyone pay his vows in the midst of storms,
when often the broken keel floats in harbour?
Or demand the prizes before the race is run,
before the seventh wheel has skilfully worn the goal?
Lying gales play favourable in love:
if any ruin comes late, it comes great.
Yet you meanwhile, though she loves you,
keep your joys shut in a silent breast.
For in love each man's own greatest words, somehow,
are wont to harm him.
Though she call you very often, remember to go once:
what causes envy is not wont to last long.
But if the age were pleasing to ancient girls,
I would be what you now are: I am conquered by the time.
Yet that age will not change my ways:
let each man know how to go his own road.
But you, who recall your services to many loves,
how great a grief tortures your eyes thus!
You have seen a tender girl of full radiance,
you have seen a dark one, each colour leads;
you have seen one come forward in Argive figure,
you have seen ours, each beauty captivates;
that one in plebeian cloak or in scarlet:
this and that is one road of an evil wound.
When one girl carries enough sleeplessness for your eyes,
one woman is enough, many ills, for anyone.

26a. I saw you in dreams, my life, with your keel broken,
